title: Tu BiShvat: planting
hookLine: many plant trees or give to planting on this day

lines: WILL YOU BE ALIVE TO EAT IT?
cards: A man walking along a road sees someone planting a carob tree. He stops and asks: how long until this tree bears fruit? Seventy years, comes the answer.
The traveler looks him up and down. And you're sure you'll be alive in seventy years to eat from it? The planter keeps digging.
That's a story from the Talmud, in tractate Taanit. The traveler is Choni, whom the same page remembers for praying down rain, and his story goes on to become something like Rip Van Winkle.
But the planter's answer is the part people quote.

teach.b: The planter says, roughly: I found this world full of carob trees. My ancestors planted them for me, so I'm planting for my children.
Then Choni sits down to eat, falls asleep, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that very tree. Are you the one who planted it?
No, the man says: my grandfather did. That's the Talmud's picture of planting: you do it for someone you may never meet.
The midrash finds the same idea in the Torah's command to plant fruit trees when Israel enters the land.

Even God, it notes, began the world by planting: Genesis says God planted a garden in Eden. So planting becomes a way of imitating God. Another teaching, in a collection called Avot of Rabbi Natan, is bolder still.
It's attributed to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: if you're holding a sapling in your hand and someone tells you the Messiah has arrived, plant the sapling first. Then go out to greet him.
Tu BiShvat became a planting day only in modern times.

The story usually told is that a teacher in the village of Zikhron Yaakov took his students out to plant trees on the fifteenth of Shevat, and the custom spread through schools and, later, tree-planting campaigns.

Today some people plant on this day, and others give money for planting. In the northern winter it's often too cold to dig, so people plant indoors, or give, or water what's already growing. Somebody planted for you.

how: Many Jews plant trees on Tu BiShvat, especially in Israel, where schools hold planting days; elsewhere many give to tree-planting funds, eat fruits of the land, or care for plants at home.

o: the new year for trees, now a day for planting
the day the first carobs are picked each year
a festival for the Temple's olive harvest

games.q: inside the planting day — tap the pairs.
p: took his students out to plant

s: Tu BiShvat planting goes back to the Mishnah
the planting custom is modern, usually traced to a teacher and his students.
when Choni woke, a grandson was gathering carobs from the tree
the planter's grandson ate from it, seventy years later.
the midrash links planting to imitating God
God planted a garden in Eden first.

games.q: you're holding a sapling. someone runs up and shouts that the Messiah has arrived. according to the teaching, what do you do?
o: plant the sapling, then go to greet him.
give the sapling to someone else.
games.why: plant it first, then go out to greet him. the work of the world isn't dropped, even for the biggest news.

practice: If there's a plant near you, give it water now, slowly, and watch the soil drink; if not, picture a tree you've loved and whoever planted it.
Then think of one person who planted something for you: a lesson, a habit, a kindness you're still eating from.

wordCard.voice: Tu BiShvat. The new year for trees, and in modern times, a day for planting what others will enjoy. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: carob, the slow tree in Choni's story.

carryVoice: Your line: plant something. The fruit may well go to someone you'll never meet. Day six hundred seventy-one, done.
